newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: PRESS DIGEST - NZ Business weeklies - May 30.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - NZ Business weeklies - May 30.

text.p: THE NATIONAL BUSINESS REVIEW

Crown Law backs heart contract: Crown lawyers have told the government the controversial contract signed for the Christchurch heart unit is enforceable, widening the already substantial rift between National and New Zealand First. Page 1.
Law change may boost power costs: Proposed law changes threaten to push up electricity prices, a report from sharebroker BZW suggests. Page 1.

SFO called in to probe tenders: The Serious Fraud Office has received an official request to investigate alleged mismanagement of the multimillion dollar New Zealand Police technology projects, Incis (Integrated National Crime Information System) and Cards (Communication And Resource Dispatch System). Page 1.

Computer costs worry ministers: This week's resignation of Accident Compensation chief executive Gavin Robins brought to the fore growing disquiet among parliamentarians about the amount of public money being spent on the computer industry.
Page 3.

'Palace' advice inadequate: The government has received inadequate advice about the costs and benefits of building the controversial $94 million ministerial palace behind the Beehive, confidential Treasury documents have revealed. Page 3.

Bhatnagar aims at the Warriors: Auckland Rugby League could decide in principle next week whether to pursue an offer from entrepreneur Roger Bhatnagar to buy the struggling DB Bitter Warriors. Page 9.

Moore survives: Pharmac general manager David Moore fought off a concerted parliamentary attack this week, claiming the agency's hard line against US drug companies had saved the taxpayer $80 million. Page 9.
Businesses snub coalition's private investment deal: Businesses are ignoring coalition agreement edicts that limit private investment in the health and energy sectors. Page 10.
Air New Zealand wins $6m aircraft overhaul contract for Chilean navy: Air New Zealand has won a US$6 million engineering contract to overhaul P3 Orion aircraft for the Chilean navy. Page 10.

Dissident fires salvo at business groups: Dissident industrialist Gilbert Ullrich has hit back at Manufacturers' Federation and Chamber of Commerce functionaries who, he says, are trying to stifle free speach over economic policy. Page 11.
Graham backs legal monopoly review: Justice Minister Doug Graham has offered grudging support for a review of lawyers' monopoly over land conveyancing. Page 11.

China sends top brass to discuss trade issues: The man who could hold the key to future Chinese investment in New Zealand arrives here this weekend to check out the climate under the Coalition government. Page 13.

Way now clear for government 'palace' despite popular outcry: The government has moved closer to the construction of the controversial $94 million ministerial "palace" building, despite mounting opposition to the project. Page 14.
Watchdog clears Xtra: Telecom's Internet operation, Xtra, has been cleared of breaching the Commerce Act. Page 15.
THE INDEPENDENT BUSINESS WEEKLY

Skellerup faces crunch point: Beleagured Maine Investments -- Murray Bolton's management buyout vehicle for Skellerup -- is facing a $7.7 million, half-yearly interest payment to bondholders in August. Page 1.
More heads to roll at ACC?: The job of a second top ACC executive, chief financial officer Ken Smyth, appears to be on the line. Page 1.

Infratil -- NZ Post bid for Argentine PO: Infratil International is about to make a joint bid -- with NZ Post, Argentine company La Caja and CEI Citibank -- for a 30-year "concession" in Encotesa, the Argentine postal service. Page 1.
Birch announces welcome tax change: Revenue Minister Bill Birch chose a KPMG client seminar in Wellington this week to announce a welcome change in the tax law. Page 3.
Ostrich man flys coop: The Savannah Ostrich Processing Company NZ Ltd, under investigation by the Serious Fraud Office, has gone into liquidation. Page 3.

Risk rises at America's Cup village: Delays in persuading America's Cup syndicates to commit to berths are making the $58 million Cup village a riskier project than the Auckland Regional Services Trust first thought. Page 3.
DB takes the brawn out of beer: DB Breweries' marketeers are wiping the macho froth off their beer ads and replacing it with a softer, more genteel finish. Page 4.

Accused tell clocked car crusador to put up or shut up: Car dealers accused on radio, tv and in the press of importing used Japanese cars with wound back speedos are telling their accuser, Dermot Nottingham, to put up some evidence to back his allegations or shut up. Page 5.
